job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Nora Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I did an accounting degree at Westmere University and finished in June. I share a room in a three-bedroom flat in the city, near the tram line, with my friend Ines, and a normal day is applications in the morning, then three hours studying for the first professional chartered exam, then a shift at a bookshop. Evenings I cook for the flat and call my mum.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the hardest part of all that, and what part do you still like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The hardest part is the uncertainty about whether the exam fees will be worth it without a firm sponsoring me. I've sent about fifty applications to accountancy firms and had four interviews. What I like is the logic of it: during my summer placement at Halden and Rowe, a mid-size firm, I prepared sales tax returns and I liked it when everything cross-checked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's reassuring, but I'd stay realistic. I'd tell friends it's a useful spreadsheet helper and nothing else, so we should keep studying and applying, the same as before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still be anxious, because the problem isn't AI, it's that firms take fewer graduates than they used to. I have some loans and about two months of money, and my parents could help in a pinch but I don't want to ask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the exam routine, sit the first paper in spring, and apply to twenty firms by Christmas, including the small ones. I'd keep the bookshop shifts. I'd use AI for formula help in Excel when I'm stuck, as I do now, and nothing fancier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like grinding along. I'm not scared, but I'm always a little behind in my head, as though I owe someone something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of the routine tasks you did at Halden and Rowe would AI plausibly take over?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Reconciling bank statements and filling in sales tax forms are the likely ones. The AI would do the first pass, and I'd check it, which could mean fewer hours billed and fewer juniors needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the exam fee do to your budget?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The fee is about 600 for the first paper, which is a week's rent plus food for me. I'd pay for it from savings if no firm sponsors me, and that's a big risk.

say: I'd say AI is a **useful spreadsheet helper** and nothing else, so we keep studying and applying.
I'd tell friends the **same plan** as before.
think: The problem isn't AI, it's that **firms take fewer graduates** than they used to.
I owe **no one anything**, but I always feel a little behind.
do: Sit the **first chartered paper** in spring and apply to twenty firms by Christmas.
Keep the **bookshop shifts** and live on a tight budget.
Use AI for **Excel formulas** when I'm stuck, as I do now.
feel: It feels like **grinding along**, with a quiet sense of being behind.
S0.quote: I'm not scared, but I'm always a little behind in my head, as though I owe someone something.
fieldNote: Nora's worry is **structural**: fewer graduate places, not the technology.
Her **exam fee** gamble is the real money risk in this world.
She uses AI **sparingly** and plainly, which fits her steady profile.

steps.text: Sit the first chartered accountancy paper in spring
Apply to twenty accountancy firms by Christmas

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big change but a manageable one. I'd say firms should train juniors to check what the AI does, not stop hiring them, and I'd say that at the next careers event.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the entry-level grunt work is mostly gone in three years. That includes the returns and reconciliations I did last summer, so firms will want fewer juniors who can check and judge. I need to be one of the few.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using AI properly for the first drafts of my study notes and for practising exam questions, then ask for placements where I'd supervise the output. I'd apply to smaller firms that might be keener to teach, and I'd keep the exam going. I'd also set up a LinkedIn page and join the local accountants' young members group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a race that has started, and I'm a few paces back. But I'm a steady runner, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a firm like Halden and Rowe look like with AI doing the first pass?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The firm would have maybe half the juniors and each one would be expected to review the output and talk to clients earlier. That makes the exams and the judgement part more valuable, and the data-entry part nearly worthless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you start using AI properly, and when?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start now, one use a week: a practice quiz, a summary of a standard, a first draft of a letter. After a couple of months I'd know where it's wrong, which is the thing a firm will pay a junior to catch.

say: I'd say firms should **train juniors to check** what AI produces, not stop hiring them.
I'd say that at the **next careers event**.
think: The entry-level **grunt work is mostly** gone in three years, so firms want fewer juniors who can check and judge.
I need to be **one of the few**.
do: Use AI for **study notes and practice** questions, once a week to begin with.
Apply to **smaller firms** that are keener to teach, and keep the exams going.
Join the **local accountants' young members** group.
feel: It feels like a **race that has started**, and I'm a few paces back but steady.
S1.quote: After a couple of months I'd know where it's wrong, which is the thing a firm will pay a junior to catch.
fieldNote: Nora sees **checking and judgement** as the value left to juniors and plans around it.
Her **steady style** shows: weekly practice, no big leaps.
She names the **fewer juniors** problem directly and sees herself in the squeeze.

steps.text: Use AI weekly to practise chartered exam questions
Apply to small accountancy firms that train juniors
Join the local young accountants' group
Keep studying for the chartered exams

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs governments and firms to move fast, and I'd say it plainly. If AI can do the thinking part within two years, then we need income support and retraining, and I'd say it to my MP.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be very worried. If thinking work is done by AI by 2028, then chartered qualifications could be worth a lot less than they cost, and my whole plan is built on them. I'd have no time to see if I'm wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably pause the exams, because 600 is a lot of money to put into a plan that could vanish. I'd look for hands-on or regulated work where a person has to sign: care admin, a local council, a trust. I'd move back with my mum for a while and put what I earn at the bookshop into savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a sinking feeling that doesn't go away. I'd be anxious at night, then practical in the morning, and then anxious again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: In the two-year picture, is it still worth paying for the exams?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd pause them, yes. It'd be a bet that the profession still needs chartered people after 2028, and I can't see the proof. I'd rather keep the 600 as a cushion for the first six months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in your life would you ring first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum, first. She doesn't understand accounting, but she understands me, and she'd have a spare room ready by the end of the call. Then Ines, who'd probably be in the same boat.

say: I'd say governments and firms must **move fast**, and I'd say so to my MP.
I'd say we need **income support and retraining** in place now.
think: Chartered qualifications could be worth **far less than they** cost, and my plan is built on them.
I'd have **no time** to see if I'm wrong.
do: **Pause the exams** and keep the 600 fee as a cushion.
Look for **regulated or hands-on work**, like council admin or care administration.
Move **back with my mum** and save everything from the bookshop.
feel: It feels like a **sinking feeling** that comes back each night after a practical morning.
S2.quote: I'd rather keep the 600 as a cushion for the first six months.
fieldNote: Nora **stops a long-term investment** because she cannot see the proof, which is rational and costly.
She leans on her **mum first**, then on a friend in the same boat.
The mood is alarmed because her **whole plan rests on** a qualification that may lose worth.

steps.text: Pause the chartered exams and keep the fee
Apply for council and care administration jobs
Move back in with my mum

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a bit like climate change: we have time, but only if we act now. I'd talk to my university careers office and say they should be teaching AI checking skills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be worried, but I think there's a way through. If I get a firm to sponsor me within a year and pass the exams by 2029, I'd have at least a couple of years of seniority before it lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep studying, but only the exams a firm is willing to sponsor. I'd take a low-paid first job if it came with training and exams, save as much as I could and keep the bookshop job until I'm sure. I'd also start learning how firms use AI for audit and tax, in a course or at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like standing at the bottom of a hill with a clear path up. It's steep, and I might slip, but it's a path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does five years change whether you'd pay for the exams?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, it changes it. With five years I'd pay for the first paper myself once, as a signal to firms, and then insist on sponsorship for the rest. In two years I wouldn't spend that money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if a firm offers you a place but the pay is low?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take it if training and exam fees were included. A low wage for two years is a fair price for a qualification, and I can live on a low wage at home.

say: I'd say we have time **only if we act** now, and careers offices should teach AI checking.
I'd tell **friends** it's a path, not a cliff.
think: If a firm sponsors me within a year, I'd have **a couple of years'** seniority before it lands.
I'm worried, but I think there's **a way through**.
do: Keep studying, but only for **sponsored exams**, paying the first paper myself once as a signal.
Take a **low-paid first job** if it includes training and exam fees.
Learn how firms use **AI for audit and** tax, in a course or at work.
feel: It feels like the **bottom of a hill** with a clear but steep path.
S3.quote: A low wage for two years is a fair price for a qualification, and I can live on a low wage at home.
fieldNote: More time lets Nora **resume the exam plan**, with sponsorship as the condition.
She is willing to **trade pay for training**, which her home situation allows.
Her mood falls a level because she sees **a visible path**.

steps.text: Pay for the first chartered paper once myself
Accept a low-paid first job that includes training
Take a course on AI in audit and tax
Keep the bookshop job until a firm confirms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is generous, and we should use it well. I'd say schools and universities should add AI auditing and ethics to accounting courses, and I'd say it without much drama.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd feel fairly settled. A decade gives me time to qualify, build a track record and be a senior person when it arrives, but I'd still keep an eye out, because it only takes one bad year to knock a plan over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get a job, qualify by about 27, and be a supervisor or an advisor by 30. I'd keep up with AI tools through work, not on my own time. I'd also save for a deposit, because a flat is a good hedge, and I'd rent out a room if I had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels okay, even a bit boring. I'm not scared, but I'm not complacent either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, how would you design the first five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first five years: first job, exams done, savings up to six months. The second five: more senior, and with enough cash to retrain if the profession changes shape.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you with so much time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would worry me is complacency. If I think ten years is a long time, I might not save or learn, and then year nine arrives and I haven't done either.

say: I'd say ten years is generous and schools should teach **AI auditing and ethics**.
think: A decade gives me time to **qualify and become senior** before the big change.
One **bad year** could still knock a plan over.
do: Get a **first job** and qualify by about 27.
Reach **supervisor or adviser** level by 30 and learn AI tools through work.
**Save for a deposit** and keep six months of cash for a retraining year.
feel: It feels **okay, even a bit** boring, with no fear but no complacency.
S4.quote: If I think ten years is a long time, I might not save or learn, and then year nine arrives and I haven't done either.
fieldNote: Nora's unease is the **gentlest** because of the long runway and her own steady habits.
She **names complacency** as her main danger.
Her plan is a **sequence**: qualify, advance, then hold cash for a retraining year.

steps.text: Get a first accountancy job and qualify by 27
Save for a deposit and keep six months in cash
Learn new AI tools through work each year

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. A qualification is a long, slow investment, and two years makes it a bad bet. What would help is firms saying honestly how many graduates they plan to hire, and exam bodies cutting fees or offering a pay-later scheme.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people in the middle, who are not rushing in or hiding, tend to get ignored. We read the news, we hedge, and we do our sums. I'd like someone to ask what the sensible option looks like.

headlineQuote: People in the middle, who are not rushing in or hiding, tend to get ignored.
portrait: Nora is a 23-year-old **accounting graduate** sharing a flat with her friend Ines, with fifty applications and four interviews but no offer.
She works at a bookshop, studies for the **chartered exams** and has some loans with about two months of savings.
She is pragmatic and middle-of-the-road, uses AI now and then, and thinks in **sums and sequences**.
Her moods follow the clock: anxious in mild worlds, alarmed at two years, and **unease at ten**.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture** worries her most, because a chartered qualification is a slow investment and two years makes it a bad bet.
whatWouldHelp: Honest **graduate hiring numbers** from firms and pay-later exam fees would help her.
